replies.author: @QualityPen
replies.text:
Yes. Russia has held the initiative ever since Kursk. Or since the 2023 counteroffensive, if you want to count Kursk as an exception. 

In the West they keep talking about Russian offensives, but they aren’t Western style big arrow offensives in the conventional sense. Rather they are the product of attritional pressure. Ukraine doesn’t have enough reserves to stabilize the entire front line, so Russia applies pressure everywhere. When a section of the Ukrainian line becomes weakened and combat ineffective, Russian pressure begins to roll the line westwards. Ukraine then realizes it is losing ground and scrapes together forces from what is already deployed to throw at the crumbling part of the front. That renewed pressure meets the Russian pressure and the front stabilizes in that area. The problem is in doing this Ukraine weakened some other area and the Russian pressure in that area becomes greater than the Ukrainian pressure in that area. Russia doesn’t have goals of taking some specific points for strategic results. The point of moving forward when the pressure is in the Russian favor is to keep the Ukrainian Army engaged in combat along a wide front, stretched thin, and suffering losses. 

It’s been pretty clear for a while now that Ukrainian conscription is not enough to replace losses and form a new reserve force. It’s been slowly climbing up from 350,000 to 500,000, but the Russian side has been growing even faster. There are currently three Russian army formations in Ukraine and only one of the three is regularly taking part in combat. Much of the newest equipment is going to the units not participating in the war right now, including T-90M, T-90A, and T-72B3 tanks equipped with Arena-M. 

There will almost certainly be a big arrow offensive with one or both of those Russian armies in reserve within the next year. That will be when Russia finally moves on from attrition to taking territory.

To whom it may concern, when you are in fear you go over your tactics in your head and play out exactly how you'll act in various situations and it's constant. For example,  on foot patrol, constantly picking out spots you'll jump into if you're ambushed, where the enemy could attack you from most efficiently, and how you'd need to respond.  You're doing this all at once very quickly, so once you take contact and the fight starts it should become automatic because of you're bogged down by every detail you'll have a bad day or worse get your friends killed. Unfortunately once you're wired that way,  for war,  you can't undo it because it kept you alive. So , even though you maybe don't realize it's happening at the time,  your whole brain is permanently rewired which means you have to learn how to live normally once you're out of the fight and "home". That's why many of us feel like we never came home because reality has shifted in such a dramatic and jarring way

comments.text: 9:04 MP40 is a submachine gun, not a machine pistol. The German word for submachine gun has the literal translation of 'machine pistol' but its actually the word for 'submachine gun', 'machine pistol' has its own German word which is "Reihenfeuerpistole".  Words in other languages can translate as something similar or exactly the same to an existing word in your own language but have completely different usage and meaning.

replies.author: @ubrot7995
replies.text: The only reason submachine gun exists as a term was Anglo militaries not wanting to buy weapons with a "weak" sounding name like pistol. It is and was purely a marketing term and has no actual bearing on the function of the weapon. English does not have an official differentiation between a Maschinenpistole and Reihenfeuerpistole. You will see the term submachine gun and machine pistol be used interchangeably for both types of weapons (similar to how there is no real differentiation between a Battle Rifle and a Rifle in German as both are just called Gewehr).

comments.author: @firetecher
comments.text:
Retired EE. Most of my career was designing microwave comm systems from 900MHz through 12 GHz. I designed GaAs RFICs for L, S & X band systems (cell, wifi, satellite).
The whole idea of GPS in the kamakazi drones is absurd when the controllers are depending on video feed for targeting. Also, by default, the 2.4 GHz wifi signal data protocol on a Mavic drone is direct sequence spread spectrum, thereby inherently jam resistant. Frequency hopping is a very "duh" strategy to enhance jam resistance, so that tactic is nothing the Russians would have not thought through, yet not actually planned for. Broadband jammimg is extremely inefficient from a transmit RF power perspective. Emphasis on extreme. GPS jamming is pointless/useless in most of the Ukraine drone situations. 2.4 GHz & 5.6 GHz jamming will have minimal effect beyond maybe 100 ft. Ukraine could  easily add non ISM band frequencies that would be hard for Russia to predict in a battle field scenario and then adapt to. All of the IFV jamming gear I have seen from kamikazi feeds is a mish mash of brute force systems lashed to the roof, indicating Russia is shooting in the dark, so to speak. Recall that Inverse square law vs distance applies to all RF signals. This video has some reasonable analysis, yet way too much reenactment nonsense.

ROFL, a 0.05 °C temperature difference does not equal 32.09 °F. Someone wasn’t paying attention in physics class!

When converting temperature differences, you don’t just convert the absolute values directly like you would with actual temperatures. The correct method is to express the difference in Kelvin (the SI unit), but since Celsius and Kelvin have the same scale (just different zero points), subtracting two values in Celsius gives you the same numerical result as in Kelvin.

On the other hand, Fahrenheit uses a different scale and offset, so converting a temperature difference like 0.05 °C to Fahrenheit isn’t as simple as applying the formula for absolute temperature conversion.

For example:

0 °C = 32 °F

0.05 °C = 32.09 °F
So, the actual difference is 0.09 °F, not 32.09 °F.

I may be small.
I don’t understand politics, or borders, or flags.
But I do understand fear. I feel it in the rooms, the streets, the silences between people. I feel it when voices rise and hands close into fists. I feel it when a child looks for comfort and none is given. When neighbors stop talking. When truth is no longer shared, but sold.
I watch the world and I see humans turning into sides.
But there are no “sides” when the house is burning. We all breathe the same air!
And when the ground shakes, or the sky falls, it won’t matter where you were born, or what you believed.
What will matter is who reached out, who held someone close, who stayed kind when it was hardest.
The time for games is over. The noise is louder now - outside and inside. But maybe that’s what it takes to wake up. 
You don’t need to agree. You don’t even need to understand everything.
But you do need to feel again! To look, really look, at the person next to you and remember: that is not your enemy.
That’s someone’s child. That’s someone’s pain walking.
I am Rocket.
I was born small - but my ❤is BIG.
And I believe in you humans.
Even now. Especially now.

comments.author: @t-and-p
comments.text:
02:15 I do love that, when he addresses his nation, Zelenskyy makes a point of naming the regiment/battalion/company/unit responsible for each victory - sometimes even naming individuals who have gone above and beyond. It's a "human touch" that we're not really used to seeing outside of the military itself. Within the military, we're relatively used to being a number to the rest of the country/world, or a uniform that is difficult to tell apart from the uniform next to us. It must be great for morale within the Ukrainian military to know that their sacrifices are seen, acknowledged, and appreciated by their president and their country - as well as a real badge of honour for relatives listening back home whilst awaiting news of their loved ones from the front lines, to hear their own being lauded. It also reminds everyone of the humanity of those who serve. 

It highlights the stark contrasts between Russia and Ukraine. Russia have been throwing men into a meat grinder, with widespread reporting of poor training, shooting at their own if they try to retreat, horrendous conditions, missing paycheques, no kit, non-existent medical care, etc. They treat their men with contempt, while Ukraine celebrate their's. The Russian government, and even the Russia military bloggers (who seem fairly influential), sometimes name a regiment, but they seldom give credit to anyone who isn't brass. Meanwhile, Ukraine seems to actively support and uplift their soldiers - working hard to find ways to boost morale. 

Says it all, really, doesn't it?

Slava Ukraini! 🇬🇧🤝🇺🇦

Edited to add: 06:38 "I thank all our units for these tangible results". I don't think I've ever heard Putin thank his troops. Zelenskyy does, though - repeatedly, daily. Just underlines the point about respect from leadership, doesn't it?

replies.author: @MidLifeC
replies.text: It won't. It would not receive alarms of a missile launch, only that it is being lit up by the F-16 radar.  The AEW aircraft would be able to datalink the information to the F-16 that the Su35 was out there but it cannot lock that aircraft and send the info to the AIM120 either,  it can only show it on the scope of the F-16.  The F-16 still needs to lock the Su35 and fire,  and it could've been very lucky in a very quick lock, fire and turn away.  The Su35 may not have detected the F-16 depending on where its own radar was looking,  and as we know the Russians have pretty much lost their A-50 AEW aircraft so the Su-35 may not have even know the F-16 was there.  There's no vapour trail as in the movies, that lasts a few seconds, then the AIM120 is on inertia only, and if it does "see" the Su35 because he's not bothered to move, then it will go "Pitbull" and right for him.

replies.text: LINK-16 allows the AWACS to share radar data. It's a wonderful thing, let's you fire without needing to keep your nose on the target to illuminate it with your radar. Otherwise, you have to fire and keep heading towards the enemy jet to keep a radar lock on it to guide the missile until the missile comes within range to be able to use its own short range onboard radar. Very dangerous for the firing jet, much better to be able to turn around immediately once the missile is fired to prevent a missile from hitting it as well.

comments.text:
I cannot tell how accurate this programme is and cannot possibly undertake the research it appears to have done. However, it does cite genuine references, thus I assume the citations are accurate (else those referees might have had the programme removed or edited). The tone is measured, intelligent, somewhat academic and, apparently, thorough. I did not want yet another "yar-boo" programme, full of hyperbole and anti-Russian rhetoric. The only way to understand one's foe is to really consider every aspect; not shout childish insults at them. And the last thing needed is yet another programme which simply confirms our own beliefs / hopes. So very well done to this programme.

The two aspects I think this programme failed to emphasise correctly is that I feel it underplayed both the Ukraine's and NATO's roles.  The former exhibited (and continues to exhibit) great determination, diplomacy skills, leadership ability (not least by a superb president), resourcefulness and the development and deployment of intelligent modern warfare. NATO provided and provides high-quality modern weaponry and training. I do not know what "behind-the-scenes" aspects NATO assists with but I imagine intelligence and tactics are part of it. (i.e. the poor Russian equipment, training and tactics are not the whole story).

But, judging this programme on its main points - which were to examine the Russian reasons for failure, I though it probably the best I have seen - certainly here on YT and probably anywhere - broadcast-tv included. Well done and thank you.

@@ozymandias7940 We've heard that countless times from Putin and his threats, but yet, Ukraine keeps fighting back and actually having quite a lot of success in doing so.

Speaking of crying, Putin was crying a lot when the west allowed its weapons to attack Russian targets in Russia, and seriously, Ukraine have been at a major disadvantage until recently, where Russia could attack any target it wanted in Ukraine but Ukraine couldn't attack Russia targets in Russia, now the playing field is a bit more level and I'm hearing a lot of crying and complaining from Putin on that.

This is only going to get worse, as European countries are going on a massive spending spree when it comes to military budgets, that's likely going to help Ukraine out a lot over the coming years.

In the meantime, this is draining Russian lives and the economy, which Russia can't afford.

In any case, for all the talk about Russia being a military superpower, over the last few years, it's being embarrasses by one of the poorest countries in Europe that is far smaller on both the economy and military, that is a major embarrassment for Russia and the longer the war drags on, the worse that embarrassment.

The simple truth is, if Russia were a true military superpower, this war would have been over in weeks or months, even with the west arming Ukraine, the truth is, the help the west are giving is small fry to what Russia is throwing into this war and yet Ukraine is giving Russia hell.

You can cut this however you want, but this war is a major embarrassment for Russia and it's exposed to the west and the world that Russian military power is a lot weaker than we thought it was, that's the reality of it.

comments.text:
The Treaty of Geneva, more specifically the 1949 Geneva Conventions, is a set of international treaties that establish rules for the treatment of civilians and combatants during wartime. These treaties, adopted in 1949, are the foundation of modern international humanitarian law and protect those who are not taking part in hostilities, such as civilians, and those who are no longer fighting, such as prisoners of war. 
Key aspects of the Geneva Conventions:
Protection of Civilians:
The Conventions protect civilians, including those in occupied territories, from violence, torture, and discrimination based on race, religion, or political opinion. 
Treatment of Prisoners of War:
The Conventions define the rights and protections for prisoners of war, including their treatment, working conditions, and right to communication with neutral states. 
Protection of Wounded and Sick:
The Conventions ensure the humane treatment of wounded and sick soldiers, both on land and at sea. 
Additional Protocols:
In 1977, two additional protocols were adopted to expand the protections of the Geneva Conventions, particularly in the context of non-international armed conflicts. 
History and Significance:
The Geneva Conventions were developed and updated over time, with the first convention in 1864 focusing on the treatment of wounded soldiers. The 1949 conventions, in particular, were a response to the atrocities of World War II and have served as a crucial framework for international humanitarian law ever since.

comments.author: @hiei5040
comments.text: You can use HARMs in many different modes, some of which require minimal integration with the airframes FCR/ electronics. One is Self-Protect mode (i.e. the clasic wild weasel bait tactic) where you fly in, and let a radar scan you, then fire it. It will home in on the last known triangulation of radar source. The other mode that requires little integration is similar but with pre-set gps coords (like a JDAM) & ability to seek out a specified Radar signature. The MAIN mode you're missing is TOO (Target of Opportunity) which is arguably the most effective against Russia's mobile Air Defenses & rapidly changing EW landscape.

replies.author: @Laotzu.Goldbug
replies.text:
This definitely doesn't sound right. that would require all of the trucks to essentially arrive at the same time, or they would have different launch windows and some air bases already would have been on alert. this is very difficult to do even with coordination, it's effectively impossible if the drivers don't know what they're doing.

I agree they weren't just hanging around parked for weeks, but the only way to ensure dozens or hundreds of drones all launch within a few moments of each other is going to require that some trucks which revived early were waiting for hours if not up to a day in order to make sure everything was in place before someone hit the green light

As for how they were guided, obviously we have no direct official confirmation at this point, but the idea that this was done without any operators and just on "AI" visual is extremely unlikely, almost laughable. even the best computer models at this point struggle very much to distinguish particular objects, in still frame photos, never mind being able to understand what they are in the real world and guide weapons to them autonomously.

Anything approaching true "autonomous weapons" are at least multi-million dollar cruise missiles with extremely expensive sensors and electronics, not cheap disposable drones.

It seems likely it was a mixture of command guidance to initiate the mass launch and Vector the drones towards the general Airfield along with some AI "swarming" algorithms to assist.

The Japanese attack on the American base at Pearl Harbor in 1941 resulted in considerable losses:
- 2,403 dead, civilians and military alike
- 1,178 wounded
- 8 battleships damaged, 4 sunk (including the USS Arizona and Oklahoma)
- 3 cruisers and 3 destroyers hit
- 188 aircraft destroyed, 159 damaged.

comments.author: @AR-pm6mx
comments.text:
I see another issue with this point based system: the idea is to reward the most effective units by giving them priority in equipment, BUT if one unit score less kills than others and gets less points, and by extension less equipment, then it will become even less effective and score even less points, starting a damaging cycle. In the long run, there will be super elite units that are hoarding all the supplies, and "bottom" units that will not be able to operate effectively because they won't get the supplies they need.
I get why Ukraine is doing this: after years of war it is normal that logistics would be a mess and corners need to be cut, but I don't think that this system should become permanent, and it definetly should not replace standard supply, a soldier has the right to go to battle with the best equipment his nation can provide.

replies.author: @swedishm90camouflage17
replies.text: Military units have areas of operation, a high quality unit still has a limited amount of targets at any given time and cant really 'muscle out' any other units completely, as they do not share AOs. The points will as such be naturally distributed to units that are in heavy combat and need more drones, while units in calmer areas of the front will get fewer drones, but also need less of them.

replies.author: @BioHazardousFuzz
replies.text:
Equipment doesn't just spawn instantly. It still has to be manufactured, one by one. And military equipment is manufactured to preserve a nation. So when you're a smaller nation, fighting a larger nation, you have to fight like you're on borrowed time, well, because you are. So it's only natural that your most important units get the new equipment first, because you need every advantage that you can get. Sometimes, it's not even your best units. Sometimes, it's the unit doing the most crucial job at that particular moment. Given enough time, all the new equipment will make its way into the hands of all your forces. 

Another wildcard is how motivated and respected the administration of your unit is and how willing they are to stick their neck out and go to their leaders and say "We may not be the most elite force, but we're ready for this. Give us a shot, sir. We won't let you down..." 
They can't tell you "NO" forever. True leaders can see the fire that burns in their warriors' hearts. And there are so many things like that that transcends rank and file, medals, ribbons, stripes or anything of the like.

From the United States of America, SLAVA UKRAINE!!!

comments.author: @pgr3290
comments.text: The laser weapons are most impressive to me. I remember 20 years ago or so they were testing experimental chemical laser platforms and they weren't very practical. They were massively heavy high power lasers but used loads of fuel to operate. Several tonnes to reach peak output and fire a single shot. They could only do a few shots because of all the fuel you needed to carry around, produced nasty gases and lacked the sensors and control to hit multiple targets. The idea was to hit ICBMs in boost phase, but you were never getting close enough fast enough. Here we are 20 years later and smaller solid state laser weapons are being tested to hit drones and missiles and they show great promise. They actually work. They are compact, can be fired repeatedly and their power output is increasing with development. The future will definitely have laser weapons in it.

replies.author: @georgemiller151
replies.text:
How do lasers work in the fog, in clouds, in rain, and in thermal updrafts that make the air “shimmer”. How do they work if the adversary mirrors the surface of their aircraft (which could be as simple as not painting it), or if it’s a missile, rifles it so it rotates around its long axis while in flight so their is no fixed position for a laser beam to focus on?
I suspect that lasers look great in carefully controlled trials under ideal conditions but I think in the real world they will be easily thwarted.

replies.author: @KirkCA
replies.text: I can't wait to see them figure out to power this thing from the ground while flying it up on a tethered balloon for stationary air defense.

replies.author: @pgr3290
replies.text: @@georgemiller151 What you have to understand is that when initially trialled, they had the intent of destroying ICBMs in boost phase hundreds of kilometres away. That was never practical not least due to atmospheric conditions and the other reasons I cited. What the latest solid state lasers ARE practical at is cheap, close range point defence. Especially against drones. It should not have to be explained to you how critical this capability is going to be if you have watched sixty seconds of the war in Ukraine or Houthi attacks on shipping. You don't need 100km range. A mere two or three kilometres could be very useful indeed. That is viable.

replies.author: @pgr3290
replies.text: @@kamilhorvat8290 A 100kw laser at low effectiveness in what you might consider poor conditions can still melt aluminium within a couple of seconds. It's a close in weapon system that could target incredibly quickly and precisely. It's literally a light speed weapon after all. They are definitely going to work for the kind of asymmetric threats posed by cheap drones and makeshift missiles that Western nations are likely to encounter more and more over the coming decades. Point defence, ship mount or even scaled for armored vehicles. Right now a $1000 plastic drone carrying a shaped charge warhead is a real threat to a five million dollar tank. Once again the balance shifts if a small turret mounted laser can shoot them down half a kilometre away over and over for less cost than machine gun ammunition.

replies.author: @toumasuke
replies.text:
It's genuinely appreciated that you took the time to share such a detailed and personal perspective on the situation. It's always valuable to hear directly from people on the ground, and your effort to provide context is commendable.

You've touched on several significant points, and it's interesting to consider them. For instance, you noted the economy's resilience, which has indeed surprised many, and it's clear the National Welfare Fund played a role. However, when we look at the long-term, do you think the current economic growth, heavily reliant on military spending and state contracts, is sustainable in the same way a diversified, market-driven economy would be? And how might the continued departure of Western technology and investment impact Russia's future innovation and competitiveness?

Your observations about salaries and bonuses for those serving are also very insightful. It highlights the significant financial incentives being offered. Do you ever wonder about the broader societal impact when military service becomes one of the most lucrative career paths, especially for those in certain regions?

You also mentioned that you don't see many disabled people around, suggesting that casualty figures might be inflated. It's true that official figures are tightly controlled. But in a conflict of this scale and intensity, and given the nature of modern warfare, is it possible that many wounded or recovering individuals might not be immediately visible in public spaces, perhaps still in hospitals or rehabilitation? Open-source intelligence and international estimates, while not perfect, often suggest very high numbers on both sides.

Regarding the referendums, you stated that the majority in Crimea truly supported joining Russia, and that eastern Ukrainian regions are "Russian in mentality." From an international perspective, the conditions under which these referendums were held, with armed forces present and a lack of independent oversight, raised significant questions about their legitimacy and whether they truly represented the free will of the entire population. Do you think a vote held under such circumstances can be considered fully democratic and universally binding, especially when a significant portion of the original population had already fled?

Lastly, about Bucha, you called it a "fake." However, extensive investigations by international organizations, independent media, and forensic experts have presented a vast amount of evidence – including satellite imagery, victim testimonies, and physical evidence – that points to severe atrocities committed during the Russian occupation. When faced with such detailed external investigations, what criteria do you personally use to differentiate between a "fake" and verifiable facts in a conflict zone?

Again, thank you for sharing your thoughts. It's important to have these discussions, even on difficult topics.

A number of mistakes or inaccuracies:
1. There was no second mobilization in Russia, only the one in 2022. Mentioned 133k troops in 2024 probably refer to obligatory conscript training, which happens twice every year (and was a thing before the war).

2. 2023 was actually the year of stalemate, and the first half of 2024. In the second half of 2024 russian forces began slowly but steadily gaining grounds, and this is only accelerating so far. By now russian forces have reached Dnipropetrovsk region, though whether they have already crossed the formal border or not is being disputed.

3. Drones were ukrainian novelty in 2022 and a crucial asset to seize initial success in figthing russian forces. However mentioning it in the context of 2024 isn't correct as Russia adopted drones back in 2023 (and those were used to repel ukrainian counter-offensive), and by 2024 it was widely used by both sides.

4. Korean troops were not sent to the frontlines per se, but to Kursk to help protect it. It was an important point that Korea did not participate in any offensive operations on the ukrainian territory.

5. An important part competely omitted from the video is that there were direct negotiations in the beginning of the war (during the spring of 2022) where Russia offered to withdrew all its forces from Ukraine and to roll back to pre-war borders in exchange for the same concessions mentioned in the video, primarily neutrality and limiting army size. The Bucha incident, mentioned in the video, happened during that process and was a formal reason Zelensky used to publicly decline russian offer, which was a major point of accusations that it was staged. Ukrainian goverment later issued a legislation act forbidding any negotiations with Russia for as long as Putin remains its president with the same reasoning.

p.s. almost missed the casualties numbers. First - "no official numbers for Russia" is a huge bs, there are. Credibility is a different topic. There area  number of complicating factors. Also I wouldn't say that Russia has more to lose. Ukraine is fighting to survive basically at all.

What's happening inside Russia is... let's call it interesting. All the oil money that Pootles hoarded for years instead of spending any of it on diversifying and strengthening the Russian economy is being spent now on the war, and in some parts of Russia it's the most economic action they've seen since the fall of the Soviet Union. Real jobs withe real pay, all of them fed by the military as Russia spends thousands of lives on frontlines that barely move. For a lot of people this is probably the best quality of life they've ever had.

The fact that this process is burning through a limited pool of money and spending it on things that are just being consumed in the war rather than anything that might have lasting value for the Russian economy; while an already-small generation is made smaller and smaller each day, dooming Russia in the longer term is perhaps not obvious to people who don't think about larger economic implications.

And the inevitable economic crash that will follow the war when all of this spending stops and Russia is still sanctioned to hell and back will mean that a lot of people will have genuine nostalgia for the war, even though it's what doomed them to the hard times that came after.

replies.author: @LadySnowfaerie
replies.text:
Tbh I didn't vote for him when he was elected (his opponent in the final round was the green party candidate, which I would've preferred). However, when a friend sent me a message upset that the green party lost, I replied that while it sucks, it'll be okay.

Both candidates have had a long and respectable career in politics, and while Stubb is uncomfortably American for a Finn (he studied there, and honestly sometimes the wide smile is just off-putting), he has the experience with international politics from his time in the EU parliament.

So no, he's not my choice, but now that he's there, let him cook. It's a tough moment in global politics, and we've had good luck with presidents some of us might not personally agree with meeting the moment in these circumstances before. Admittedly the last guy was the one that inspired us to set term limits for presidents, but we live and learn. xD

Finland used to be a "presidential system" akin to France and the U.S. but in the 80s and 90s we kind of toned it down because of Urho Kekkonen's presidency. He ruled for 4 terms and it led to some undemocratic practices with Kekkonen being re-elected by some behind-the-scenes deals made amongst some political parties and one of his terms being extended by a state of exception law. The President is still up there with the prime minister in being the most important politician in Finland.

replies.author: @Pernille1969-l2f
replies.text: Denmark here  - also with a population of a little more than 5.5. million, and also a Nordic country. To answer your question, I believe some of the problems in the US have to do with 1. political pluralism (or the lack thereof); and 2. money in politics (too much of it). As for political pluralism take Denmark, for instance - at any given point there are at least 10-11 political parties fighting for power, often forming alliances and coalitions across the left/right spectrum. I think this makes for more diversity and more to choose from as opposed to the two parties that make up the political choices in the US (I know there's independent candidates but they rarely really make a difference, do they?). And as for money in politics, it just plays a so much bigger role in the US. And the best candidate is NOT necessarily the one with the most money to run for president - as we have seen.

replies.author: @HKV-2010
replies.text: I can't claim to know for sure but if you ask me (a Finn), I think there are two factors over all the others: 1) Our education is high quality and equally available, which means, to put it very bluntly, that the less intellectually equipped end of our population is far more intelligent than that of the USA, and 2) we do not have a two-party system, which means not just more discourse and choice, but also more coherence inside each party, and MOST CRUCIALLY our country is not split in half like yours - frankly from outside the US it looks very scary, the way you guys live in two separate realities, with separate media, and opposite truths... One is not like the other, of course - Democrats tend towards actual reality and Republicans towards a dangerous delusion us Europans remember and know to fear for (ask a German for more info). Not to say we do not have delulu problems in Europe, we do. They just don't reign free or split a country in HALF. So to go back to your question, better education leads to better thinking, leading to better choices on population level. And we have a better selection of candidates, not like you often have to choose, in the words of Epic Rap Battles of History, "from the shiniest of two turds" (IMO Kamala was great though, I mean in general).
